purpose: Map the high-density biblical chain around women mourning a dead/disappeared male figure, gates, tombs, removed stones, absent bodies, return, gardener imagery and socially marginal women, then compare those motifs to the Tim Dooley Son/Thomas archive without treating resemblance as prediction or proof.
method_rules: Project-side event first; biblical comparator second.
Keep direct textual overlap distinct from later symbolic synthesis.
Do not identify modern people with biblical figures merely because roles overlap.
Do not repeat the traditional but textually unsupported claim that Mary Magdalene was a prostitute; the New Testament does not call her one.
For Sammy, preserve 'lady of the night' only as the user's characterization unless independently documented.
Rank dense multi-motif sequences above single-word coincidences.

new_relational_findings.finding: Ezekiel 8 and Luke 7 create a notable two-gate structure: at one gate women mourn Tammuz; at another gate a woman mourns her dead only son, who is then raised. The project independently carries North Gate + woman mourning Thomas/Tammuz + Son-return language.

Matthew 27 places women opposite the newly sealed tomb; Mark 16 places women returning and explicitly asking who will roll the stone away; John 20 places a woman at the removed-stone tomb weeping over the missing body. Read together, the Synoptic/John tradition yields women witness burial → stone closure → women return → stone moved → body absent → recognition/return.

John 20 places a mourning woman at an emptied tomb, then has her mistake the returned Jesus for the gardener before Jesus speaks of ascending to the Father. This creates a later textual chain Tomb → Woman/Weeping → Missing Body → Gardener → Recognition → Father that strongly overlaps project vocabulary while remaining a comparison rather than identity claim.

The project still lacks a securely recovered contemporary 'rolled stone' statement, but Matthew 27, Mark 16 and John 20 together provide placement + question + removal of the tomb stone. Stone should remain 'biblical-side confirmed / project-side unresolved' until a dated Tim/Son source is recovered.

Jeremiah 31 supplies a separate Hebrew-Bible grammar: woman weeps because children are no more, followed by a promise of return. This makes mourning → disappearance/absence → return a recurring biblical form beyond the Gospel tomb stories.

Across Ezekiel 8, Luke 7, Luke 23, Matthew 27, Mark 16 and John 20, women are not incidental scenery: their mourning or watching marks death, burial, boundary crossing, absence, recognition or restoration. This makes Sammy's role as a mourning commenter structurally more relevant than treating her only as a peripheral character.

Rahab and Tamar show that socially stigmatized or sexually marginal female figures can occupy decisive positions in biblical narrative and even genealogy. This supports a broad cultural comparator for Sammy's user-described social role, but not a one-to-one biblical identity.
